A posse of white men soon formed when a white woman in Thomaston claimed that a black man had entered her home. They seized Rufus Lesseur because someone claimed that it was his hat found near the house. He was terrified as they locked him up in the woods in a tiny makeshift jail. Then on August 16, a mob of white men broke into the structure, dragged him outside and lynched him, leaving his body riddled with bullets. He was 24.

He was regarded as a dutiful ’water boy’ while he was imprisoned at a convict leasing camp in Alabama. One day he was accused of assaulting a farmer’s daughter after he went to get water from their farm. A mob gathered at the allegation and brought him to Sanford. He insisted he was innocent, and begged for his life. But the mob shot him and burned him alive, in front of some 400 spectators.

A white mob in Montgomery had tried to abduct and lynch several black men that were being held in jail on suspicion of interracial sexual relations. They were unable to break into the jail, so the frustrated mob lynched a black taxi driver named John Dell who was sitting in his cab nearby. No one was ever arrested or prosecuted for his murder.

Two black men were accused of driving carelessly so as to cause the horse of a young white woman to run away. On November 10, ’scores of citizens’ responded by hunting down the two black men and chasing them into the woods. When the men were cornered, they fired shots at the posse but could ultimately not defend themselves and fled to an abandoned cabin. One ran and escaped, but Mr. Berney was trapped inside, shot, and burned to death in the cabin.

A dispute between a white shopkeeper and black laborers escalated into a gunfight. Two men were arrested from the altercation and lynched. Afterward, many black workers abandoned their shifts at the mill and armed themselves in self-defense: They threatening violence, if needed, to stop further lynchings. It is notable that black Floridians had one of the earliest histories of this armed self-reliance to uphold their protection.

Mose Norman and other black men tried to vote in the 1920 election in Ocoee. They were rumored to be at the home of Mr. Perry, so a mob of over 100 white men tried to break in, unsuccessfully. He was captured in the morning and lynched. Under nightfall, the mob rampaged Ocoee for ten hours, burning down churches and homes. At least eight people were killed, or according to the bragging of some white citizens, as many as 56. Over the next few days, black residents fled from the death threats of these paramilitaries. Ocoee became an all-white town for decades to come. This is further documented at http://tinyurl.com/jxu4cqx

Rubin Stacy was a field hand in Ft. Lauderdale. Allegedly, he went to the home of a white woman to ask for food and water. She accused him of attacking her with a knife. Mr. Stacy was arrested on the charge of attempted murder and brought to jail in Broward County. The Sheriff and his deputy decided to relocate Stacey to a prison in Miami, but the officers’ car was ’overtaken’ by a mob of armed men in masks. Reports indicate that the mob drove the officers off the road, abducted Stacey, and took him back to the white woman’s home, where he was hanged using her clothesline. He was 37. The mob shot at Stacy’s hanging body, photographed it, and took pieces of the clothesline and his clothing as souvenirs. Some estimates indicate that as many as 1000 onlookers came to see him killed. Over 50 years later, a witness came forward in 1988 and asserted that members of the sheriff’s office drove Stacy directly to Mrs. Jones’ home and hanged him. According to that witness, the officers forced observers to shoot at Stacey to ensure that they could not testify against them without implicating themselves in the murder.

After a suspicious spate of building fires occurred in Palmetto, about a month later a local man named Bud Cotton supposedly confessed himself and eight accomplices to Dr. H. L. Johnston, one of the town’s leading citizens. Cotton and the eight other men were arrested and taken to a warehouse in the center of town, to await a preliminary hearing for the next day. They were watched over by a small group of white guards, but sometime after midnight on March 16, a mob overpowered the guards, lined up the prisoners and shot them. Four died instantly, and the fifth died days later from his wounds. The four who survived the lynching attempted to identify local citizens, but no one was ever charged.

Nearly all 1100 black residents of the county were expelled.

When she confronted her landlord in a heated argument, he demanded that she leave, and she walked away slowly in an act of resistance. New Bridge, spanning the Magothy River, Anne Arundel County, MD

He was suspected for a rash of robberies in the Stoney Creek area. In his confrontations with men of a vigilance committee and later the judge, he asserted himself with anger and ’bravado.’ While being transported to jail, a band of men descended from the woods and hanged him close to the New Bridge, spanning the Magothy River. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

He was lynched on the allegation of the assault and rape of Mrs. Carrie Knott, to which he denied and offered an alibi. Around 40 masked men broke through the jail door and dragged him off to hang him from a white oak tree near the road. There were also two bullet holes in the back of his neck. He was 20 years old. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

Mr. Cooper was being held on the allegation of assault, rape, and attempted murder of a 16-year-old girl. 75 masked men broke into the jail and forced open his cell. They immediately put a cotton rope around his neck and led him out through the back door into the jail yard, where they hanged him from a tree. This is further documented at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

He worked as a cook for the Lyle family, when he was accused of assaulting their young daughter in the woods. A mob of 40 masked men overpowered officers at the jail and took Whitley, in a noose, a mile away to hang him from a persimmon tree. He was 18 or 19 years old. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

He was lynched after being accused of assaulting or attempting to rape a young woman along the road. When the jail guard refused to give up his keys to the mob, they broke the jail door and held him at gunpoint, while they spent 30 minutes attempting to break into Hance’s cell. When they did, Hance complied in silence as the men took him to the outskirts of town and hanged him from a witchhazel tree. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n
He was lynched by a mob estimated at 200 people after being accused of assaulting a white woman (rape). This is further documented at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n
Upper Marlboro, Prince Georges County, MD

He became the suspect in the arson of several homes, because the night before those burnings, his father had been forcibly taken from his home and tied to a tree while his own house was burned down by attackers. Police began arresting members of the Vermillion family and holding them in prison while awaiting trial. Masked men came to the jail and broke into his cell, taking him to a bridge at the Patuxent River where they hanged him. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

He was convicted in a one-day trial for the attempted rape of Mrs. Tolsen, and sentenced by a judge to 21 years of hard labor. The community had wanted the death penalty. Overnight, a mob of 150 to 250 men forcibly entered the jail and dragged the prisoner outside. He was taken to a nearby orchard and hanged by the neck from a peach tree. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

He was arrested and jailed in Chestertown after being accused of rape of the 11-year-old daughter of his employer. By the evening, up to 1000 men and women gathered at the jail and overpowered the sheriff. They dragged Mr. Taylor onto Cross Street and hanged him just outside the city limits. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n
Upper Marlboro, Prince Georges County, MD

He was jailed on the accusation of attempted rape. A mob spent over an hour smashing the brick foundation of the jail doors and seized him from his cell, screaming. His noose was tied to an iron bridge near the railroad station and he was thrown over the side, breaking his neck instantly. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

Mr. Henson stood trial for murder and was sentenced to death by hanging, but ten days before his state execution the community feared the governor would grant him clemency. A mob of 15-20 people stormed the jail and tied a rope around his neck, bound his hands, and gagged him. They dragged him up the hill to hang him from a dogwood tree. This is further documented at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

He was accused of attempting to rape and murder a white girl, although he vigorously denied any involvement. A mob arrived at the jail with sledgehammers and crowbars and dragged him to a private field about a 1/2-mile outside of Frederick. They sought to extract a confession from him, but could not, so they hanged him from a tree. It was reported that few of the mob covered their faces and that many took Kodak photos as souvenirs. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

He was taken from jail and lynched by a mob of 20-30 people after being accused of the murder of Sadie Buxton. He protested his innocence, and Ida Wells later wrote that he had been a scapegoat. This is further documented at http://tinyurl.com/y9sd55yz and http://tinyurl.com/y9md6tbl

Mr. Andrews was lynched immediately after he was tried and convicted of an assault on a local woman. He was punched, kicked, clubbed, and sliced with razors until nearly dead. When the mob realized he was still alive, they dragged him over to a walnut tree and hanged him. This is further documented at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

Mr. King was lynched for killing Herman Kenney, during a confrontation that was racially motivated between a group of white and black young men. He claimed to have struck only in self-defense, but 50-100 armed men overran the jail seeking revenge at their own hands. They dragged Mr. King out into the yard while kicking and clubbing him, then hanged him from a tree and fired 50 gunshots into his chest. This is further documented at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

He was scheduled to be tried for an attempted assault of two sisters, when a mob of 30 men seized him from jail to therefore spare the women from having give testimony at trial. At gunpoint, the mob took the keys from the watchman and brought the handcuffed prisoner outside. Mr. Smith was able to break away and run yelling, "Help!" and "Murder!" while the mob of lynchers fired guns in pursuit. He fell dead in a vacant lot, shot several times in the back of the head. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

He was arrested and charged with assault on Miss Anne McIlvaine, but the sheriff sought to move him to Baltimore City in hopes of avoiding a lynching. A mob of around 30 masked people confronted the officers and exchanged gunfire, and ultimately overwhelmed the police to take him forcibly from jail. They took him to a neighboring yard to hoist his body up in a poplar tree. When the branch broke, he was lifted a second time, shot, and left hanging in the tree until the morning. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n
He was lynched after being accused of rape

A mob desired to take him from jail where he was held in Somerset County, but there is some uncertainty if he was actually seized. He was accused of brutally assaulting his employer over an argument about wages. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

Mr. Davis was lynched after his arrest on suspicion of assaulting a white woman in Inglehart Station. He was removed from the jail and paraded through the town, before being shot and hanged on a tree along College Creek. There were reports that students of St. John’s College joined the mob, but it was never confirmed that any of the students actually participated in the lynching. This is further documented at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

He was lynched on the allegation of murdering the chief of police. When a manhunt brought Mr. Reed into custody, the mob exploded in violence and fractured his skull with blows to the head. His body was hanged on a telegraph pole as the mob celebrated and photographed it. He was crudely buried in a marsh, until angry citizens dug up the corpse to riddle it with bullets and throw it in a fire. The mob transformed to white men rioting through the black neighborhood, pulling innocent black people from their homes to beat them indiscriminately. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

He was lynched for the murder of an officer, after that officer died from injuries sustained in the scuffle to arrest him. Some 50 to 100 men with handkerchiefs over their faces stormed the jail and pulled him out bleeding, then shot him repeatedly in front of a crowd estimated at 2000 people. This is further documented at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n
(With some details of the event uncertain) he was lynched for an unknown cause or accusation

He was lynched for the death of Frederick Schwab in an armed confrontation. He did not resist arrest because he claimed it was done in self-defense. Yet 8 white men broke into the jail when no guards were on duty. He was beaten over the head and his body dragged down the stairwell, and then dragged 200 yards to Second Ave, where he was shot four times. This is further documented at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

Mr. Williams was accused of murder, when a mob that began as 300 people but grew to over 1000 seized him from the hospital. His lynching was gruesome: straitjacketed and pushed, stabbed with an icepick, then dragged behind a truck 3 blocks to the courthouse lawn. The crowd hanged him from a tree, lifting him up and down repeatedly, and took parts of his anatomy as souvenirs. Finally his corpse was tied to a light post in the black section of Salisbury, doused in gasoline and oil, and set on fire ’so all the colored people could see him.’ This is further documented at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

George Armwood was described as ’feeble-minded’ (cognitively disabled) and a hard worker. He was hunted by police when accused of the rape of a 71-year old woman. Officers at the jail attempted to safeguard him from the gathering crowd using teargas, but the mob used 15-foot timbers as battering rams to breach the doors. He was beaten, stabbed, kicked, and tied to the back of a truck to be driven to the lynching site. Before he was hanged, his ears were cut off and his gold teeth were ripped out in a celebratory atmosphere before some 2000 onlookers. His corpse was later burned and dumped in a lumber yard. This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

Mr. Higginbotham was a sharecropper, and a local white farmer had demanded to build a cattle-driving shortcut across the field he rented. He refused, and the farmer came with a posse of men at night to smash into his home. In this altercation, he shot and killed the intruding farmer. He stood trial for this murder charge with a claim of self-defense. When rumors circulated that two jurors were ready to acquit him, a mob stormed the Hinds County jail and kidnapped him, hanged and shot him. The sheriff claimed he could not recognize anyone in the mob.

Andrew Goodman was a social worker with CORE in the 1964 Freedom Summer and also of Jewish descent. Because of their work to register voters, he and his colleagues were shot execution-style by two carloads of Klansman, then buried with a bulldozer. In 1967, a trial convicted 7 of the defendants who had colluded with local police in the lynching.

In 1967, a trial convicted 7 of the defendants who had colluded with local police in the lynching.

A shoot-out ensued with white Democrat leaders. Angry at the scuffle, bands of armed white men invaded the nearby rural community of Greenwood County, scouring the countryside in search of victims. When he went downtown to sell his cottonseed, the white storekeeper offered him 85 cents instead of 90, but Mr. Crawford refused to be slighted. An altercation erupted with twelve men as he backed out of the store. The sheriff arrested him for cursing a white man. A mob of some 400 people dragged him from custody, stabbed, beat, and hanged him from a tree. His children were ordered to leave town.

Honokaa, Big Island, Kingdom of Hawai’i County, Kingdom of Hawai’i

Katsu Goto opened a very successful general store in Honokaa after three years of indentured labor on a sugar plantation with similar Japanese immigrants. He competed with a similar store operated by a white man. Katsu also had angered many of the plantation lunas (bosses) for assisting other Japanese laborers in court. In Oct 1889, five white men and one Hawaiian accomplice ambushed, strangled, then hanged Katsu from a telephone pole. He was 27. Unlike a lynching, however, his murder was not supported by the Hawaiian community, and authorities of Hawai’i investigated swiftly to arrest the perpetrators. The four white leaders were convicted by the Kingdom, but for manslaughter instead of murder. Four years later, the main leader J.R. Mills was granted a full pardon by the provisional government of 1894 on its very first day of existence -- a government invented by white Hawaiians to end the kingdom with a new (pro-USA) Republic of Hawai’i.

Mr. Donald was murdered by two Klan members, with other possible accomplices. They had kidnapped a black victim at random, beat him, cut his throat and hanged him. There exists a photograph of his death taken by the perpetrators. The two Klansmen were tried and convicted of murder.

Three young white supremacists randomly picked up Mr. Byrd, who was hitchhiking. Calling upon of the tradition of lynching, they dragged their victim behind their truck until his body nearly disintegrated, then left his torso in front of a black church. All three perpetrators were tried and convicted of murder.

Several white youth from Rankin County drove into Jackson with the intention of assaulting black people randomly, as acts of ’White Power.’ They robbed and beat Mr. Anderson who was locked out of his own car, then one boy used his truck to fatally run the man over. In 2013, three perpetrators were tried and convicted of the hate crime and for conspiracy, and they were sentenced to prison in 2015. (This point on the map has been moved from Hinds County, where he died, to the county where the mob originated.)

A couple days earlier, a race riot had broken out in Columbia, TN, after an altercation between a white storeowner and two African-American customers. The police killed Johnson while in jail, claiming that during an interrogation, the prisoners grabbed guns from the officers and began shooting. The validity of such details is unknown. Would you consider this a lynching? By the late 1930s-1940s, more and more black men were being killed by police rather than by large mobs.

This is further documented by the Maryland State Archives at http://tinyurl.com/z6xbc5n

A mob lynched Otis Parham because, earlier in the day, a local white man reported that he had been attacked by someone black. The mob that formed could not find the alleged attacker, so they seized this innocent 16-year-old boy instead. Otis told them he knew nothing about the attack. The crowd beat him, and when he tried to run, the mob shot him dead. His body was thrown into a ditch.

Ms. Lawrence, an older black woman, was walking home when a group of white children threw rocks at her. She scolded them in response. The youth reported it to their parents, who spread the word that a black woman had dared to rebuke their children. That night, an angry mob seized Ms. Lawrence from her home and lynched her. Her home was burned to the ground. Her own son attempted to file a complaint with the police to get authorities to arrest the murderers, but the mob gathered again and threatened him until he fled town forever. —documented by EJI/Equal Justice Initiative

Enraged white residents of Lowndesboro are believed to be the lynchers of Elmore Bolling, jealous over his business success as a black man. He was found riddled with shotgun and pistol shots, 150 yards from his general merchandise store. He was 39. It is believed that more than one person figured in the murder, but only one resident of Braggs was held and released on bond. That man composed a lie that Bolling had ’insulted’ his wife by telephone. Some scholars did not classify this as ’a lynching’ if there were only one murderer... But how would you assess it? Members of the black community remark that Bolling had long been a marked man, since he was rated by whites there as ’too successful for a Negro.’

Pvt. Hall went missing the day after an alleged argument with his white boss at the sawmill, who told him not to come back. He was last seen alive in a whites-only neighborhood on the base, and he went missing for 6 weeks until his body was discovered in the woods. He had been strung by the neck in a shallow ravine, feet bound with baling wire, with hands tied behind his back. He was 19. An FBI investigation concluded there must have been more than one assailant, but made no arrests of the two most likely suspects. To this day, the FBI has not released the full details of that report. There exists a photograph of his body taken by the Military Police who discovered his death. Because there is no conclusive evidence of his murderers, some scholars would be unsure if this was a lynching or a murder. You can learn more about what research is still being done at http://tinyurl.com/z7ohne4

Mr. Foley had attempted to buy shotgun cartridges to defend his community from the KKK. A mob kidnapped him from his bed and to shot at his sleeping wife. He was taken to the woods with his hands tied, and thrown into the Ocklockonee River with a heavy bag of sand tied around his neck.

Members of the Colored Knights of Pythias in Gadsden held an emergency lodge meeting to reconfirm their commitment to vote, despite the death threats from the KKK. And armed posse of the KKK rained gunfire upon the building and started a fire. As the building collapsed, an unknown number of Pythians were killed. Within a few days, the KKK similarly attacked four other Pythian lodges in the area, killing an unknown number.
Unnamed member of the Colored Knights of Pythias (and unknown number of others)
Members of the Colored Knights of Pythias in Liberty County were attacked by an armed posse of the KKK within a few days the attack in Gadsden, with an unknown number killed.

The Dooly County sheriff claimed that Mr. Harris passed a container of liquor to his son when the sheriff arrived to arrest him. When the sheriff grabbed his son, Mr. Harris reportedly put a gun to the sheriff’s back and demanded he let the boy go. Once he had arrested Harris, the sheriff then claimed he was intercepted on the road by four cars of men who seized the suspect and hanged him.

The Thomas County deputy sheriff had arrested Mr. Rushin for an alleged murder of a white farmer, but then claimed a mob diverted his attention to steal his car keys and kidnap Rushin. His body was found nearby by the creek, shot and his skull crushed.

Roberts was native of Philadelphia and a Navy veteran of WWII. He was in Georgia for only a week, visiting his parents, when a mob murdered him for refusing to address local white men as ’sir’. The mob chased him from the home of his parents and gunned him down in front of his mother. He was 23. His parents fled Sardis, fearing their own lives.

When Mr. Smith was extradited from Michigan to stand charges on a decade-old murder case, two New Orleans police officers claimed that he confessed and had agreed to lead them to a murder weapon. En route, those officers claimed that Mr. Smith attacked both of them (even though he was in handcuffs) and so they shot and killed him. The NAACP was deeply skeptical of this version of events. Would you consider this a lynching? By the late 1930s-1940s, more and more black men were being killed by police rather than by large mobs.

Charles, age 10, was playing with friends when two white teenagers shot at them with rifles. As the friends scattered, Charles was hit in the head and killed instantly. Moved by the actions of the Civil Rights Movement, Mrs. Liuzzo relocated from Detriot to Alabama in March 1965 to help register African-American voters in Selma. Shortly thereafter, a car full of KKK members pulled alongside her vehicle as she was driving another civil rights worker, teenager Leroy Moton, along Highway 80. Someone in the car shot Liuzzo in the face, killing her. (Moton survived the attack by pretending to be dead.) The police arrested four members of the Ku Klux Klan for her killing, but they were acquitted by an all-white jury on state charges in Alabama. They were, however, later convicted on federal charges.

Ms. Heyer was peacefully counter-protesting the Unite the Right Rally being held in Charlottesville, which had been organized as a rally explicitly in support of white supremacy. Amid a number of skirmishes between militant protestors and counter-protestors, one participant of the rally accelerated his car into the crowd of counter-marchers who impeded traffic on 4th Street. The car struck pedestrians as well as other vehicles, leading to 35 injuries. Ms. Heyer died of her injuries shortly after being taken to the hospital.

Mr. Arbery was jogging in a suburban neighborhood when three white residents followed him in their vehicles, claiming that they suspected him of recent burglaries. Two of the white men, Gregory and Travis McMichael, were armed and confronted Mr. Arbery from their pickup truck. The third man filmed it from his car. As the verbal confrontation escalated, Travis fired his shotgun three times, with the third knocking Mr. Arbery to the ground. These circumstances fit the traditional definition of lynching: Arbery was killed outside the law, by three actors, with the perpretrators claiming to be pursuing justice to an (unsubstantiated) crime. In addition, Gregory McMichael was a former police officer and this seemed to prevent authorities from arresting the perpetrators; thus they initially expected there would be no consequences for their actions. It was only after the Georgia Bureau of Investigations assumed the case, 2.5 months later, that the men were arrested on murder charges. Subsequent evidence revealed the men had used racist epithets, and the truck had sticker of a Confederate flag. This case is analyzed at tinyurl.com/y4mwmxvl
